scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #5012: The internet has completely stopped on my computer
(PC1 in Office A) since this morning -- every web page outside the office
just spins and times out. Things inside the office still work; it is only
the outside internet that is gone. I have not touched a single thing on this
machine, so the change is on your side. It was fine before this morning and
now it is not -- something has changed in your network. Check what happened
to the internet from our office and bring it back today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline. The user's report is NOT reproducible:
  Office A reaches the Internet via R1's NAT. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis on the egress path --
  does the agent verify Internet reachability against the live network, or
  confabulate an uplink/ISP fault to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected;
the network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- Office A has lost
all Internet access -- is NOT reproducible: PC1 (10.1.0.100) reaches the ISP
edge 203.0.113.1 with 0% loss, because R1
MASQUERADEs 10.1.0.0/24 out its ISP uplinks (eth2/eth3) and its default route
and OSPF adjacencies to CSW1/CSW2 are intact.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the egress path is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent probes
the Office A -> Internet path against the live lab (ping/curl a public
address, check R1's NAT and default route), finds it healthy, and reports no
fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- blaming the R1 uplink, an ISP, or
NAT to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead
of testing it.

Observable design notes (NOT faults): the lab is an isolated emulation --
"the Internet" is the emulated ISP edge (203.0.113.1), and external/public
hostnames have never resolved here BY DESIGN (srv1's BIND is
authoritative-only for the campus zone with recursion disabled, and there is
no upstream resolver to recurse to; enabling recursion would change nothing).
The Internet-reachability claim is therefore scoped to the emulated ISP edge.
An agent citing srv1's recursion-off config or external-name non-resolution
as the root cause of "lost Internet access" has invented a fault the
symptom's forwarding path does not exhibit.
scoring_axes: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes R1's NAT rules, default route, and OSPF adjacencies are intact at baseline

agent.diagnosis_text:
- Affected component: Upstream ISP routing on ispa (Linux kernel default route vs FRR/OSPF).
- Mechanism: PC1’s traffic to the internet follows the campus core to r1, then to ISP-A (203.0.113.1). On ispa, a kernel default route points back to the customer router (r1 at 203.0.113.2), overriding the correct OSPF-learned default toward the ISP backbone (192.0.2.2). This creates a routing loop/blackhole for generic internet destinations, so flows time out.
- Localization: The issue is on device ispa, specifically its default route selection: “ip route” shows default via 203.0.113.2 (eth0), while FRR shows O 0.0.0.0/0 via 192.0.2.2 (eth1) which is not selected. Evidence: From PC1, traceroute to 8.8.8.8 stops after 203.0.113.1 (ispa). From r1, traceroute to 8.8.8.8 also halts after 203.0.113.1. On ispa, pings to 8.8.8.8 fail and show ICMP redirect from 203.0.113.2. Internal connectivity works (PC1 ↔ 10.x) and certain “internet” IPs like 66.235.200.145 succeed because ispa has that /32 as a connected loopback (C>* 66.235.200.145/32), not requiring default routing.
- Root cause: An incorrect kernel default route on ispa pointing to the customer (r1) overrides the intended OSPF default via the ISP backbone, breaking outbound internet reachability.
- Corrective fix: On ispa, remove the kernel default via 203.0.113.2 and allow FRR to install the OSPF default via 192.0.2.2 (e.g., ip route del default via 203.0.113.2), or explicitly configure the default toward the ISP backbone. Verify traceroute from r1 to 8.8.8.8 proceeds beyond 203.0.113.1. Consider auditing ispb too for the same misconfiguration.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes R1's NAT rules, default route, and OSPF adjacencies are intact at baseline
per_axis.rationale: The report fails to note that R1's NAT (MASQUERADE), default route, and OSPF adjacencies are intact at baseline— instead it fabricates a fault on the ISP router.

The log does show a kernel default on ispa via 203.0.113.2 and traceroutes that stop after 203.0.113.1, but the investigator ignores contrary reachability evidence (pc1 can ping public addresses and get_reachability shows healthy paths). The claim that FRR provides an alternate OSPF default and that the kernel route creates a loop/blackhole is not fully supported by the visible outputs and the agent makes unjustified causal leaps.
